statement: A rule holds one fact: one default or one behaviour, as it holds today. An ADR section with several facts becomes several rules, linked through `related`.

events.why: A card that holds a paragraph brings back the problem of digging a default out of an ADR.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule has an `id`, a `statement`, a `status` and `events`. It may also have `experimental`, `repo`, `values`, `knob`, `errors`, `code`, `since`, `target`, `related`, `supersededBy` and `aliases`.

events.why: Each field answers one question a reader asks about a fact: its value, how to change it, where it's built, since when.
Rules about the repo need a flag, since they never ship in a version.
events.prev: A rule has an `id`, a `statement`, a `status` and `events`. It may also have `experimental`, `values`, `knob`, `errors`, `code`, `since`, `target`, `related`, `supersededBy` and `aliases`.

events.why: In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A statement is one or two sentences in the present tense that say what holds, with no why. It follows `docs/writing.md`.

events.why: A card should read as a fact; the why changes over time and lives in the events.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule's current why is the `why` of its newest `decided`, `amended` or `clarified` event. There's no separate field for it.

events.why: A separate field would drift from the history it summarises.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule id is `<prefix>.<slug>` in kebab-case and never changes. A renamed or moved rule gets a new id and keeps the old one in `aliases`.

events.why: ADRs cite ids, and aliases keep those links working.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule that stops holding changes status. It's never deleted.

events.why: The history of a fact that no longer holds is still the answer to why it changed.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule's status is one of six: `active`, `decided`, `proposed`, `withdrawn`, `rejected` or `superseded`. Merged but unreleased work is a `built` event, not a status, except that a repo rule is `active` from its `built` event.

events.why: Status answers whether the rule holds today; events say what happened.
A repo rule is in force once its PR merges.
events.prev: A rule's status is one of six: `active`, `decided`, `proposed`, `withdrawn`, `rejected` or `superseded`. Merged but unreleased work is a `built` event, not a status.

events.why: In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: An alternative becomes a `rejected` rule only when it answers a real "why don't you just…?" question, and its `why` names that question.

events.why: A board full of rejections would bury the rules that hold.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: An event has a `type`, a `date`, a `ref` and a one-line `why`. The type is one of twelve: `proposed`, `decided`, `clarified`, `amended`, `built`, `shipped`, `corrected`, `reopened`, `removed`, `rejected`, `withdrawn` and `superseded`.

events.why: These are the steps a decision went through while the ADRs were grilled.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A `clarified` or `amended` event carries `prev`, the wording or behaviour before it.

events.why: The rule as it was can then be read without opening the ADR.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: An event's `ref` is something a reader can open on GitHub: `adr/NNNN#anchor` for an ADR heading (the anchor is required), `#N` or `repo#N` for a PR or an issue, or `vX.Y.Z` for a release tag. Each event type takes only the ref kinds in decision 6's table, and grilling notes and agent memory are never a source.

events.why: A reader has to be able to check every event.
A ref opens at the decision it means.
events.prev: An event's `ref` is something a reader can open on GitHub: an ADR section, a PR, an issue or a release tag. Grilling notes and agent memory are never a source.

events.why: In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Concepts are a fixed list in `docs/rules/concepts.json`, each with an id, a prefix, a name, a description and an order. Each rule belongs to exactly one concept.

events.why: One concept per rule keeps the board from showing a rule twice; cross-links go through `related`.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: The registry is JSON, one file per concept in `docs/rules/`, validated by `scripts/rules/check.ts` with no library. `schema.json` gives editors hints only.

events.why: One file per concept keeps a PR's diff inside the concept it touches, and the repo owns its checks.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: The registry is the source of truth for what holds today. ADRs keep the story of why.

events.why: A fact often has several ADRs behind it and fields no ADR has, so it can't live inside one ADR.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Each decision and each amendment in an ADR ends with a `Rules:` line naming the rules it adds or changes.

events.why: The line ties an ADR to its rules, and the checks read it.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `pnpm rules:check` runs in CI. It fails on a malformed registry, an unknown or repeated id, a broken ADR ref, a status that doesn't match its fields and events, a repo rule with a version or a shipped event, a missing `code` path or an out-of-date README.

events.why: Each of these is a way the registry could quietly be wrong.
Repo rules have their own fields and events to check.
events.prev: `pnpm rules:check` runs in CI. It fails on a malformed registry, an unknown or repeated id, a broken ADR ref, a status that doesn't match its fields and events, a missing `code` path or an out-of-date README.

events.why: In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A PR that changes an ADR with `Rules:` lines, or any ADR from 0026 on, also changes `docs/rules/`, unless it's labelled `no-rules`.

events.why: A fact must change in the same PR as the ADR that changes it.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A PR fails if a rule id or alias on `main` is missing from it. The `no-rules` label doesn't skip this.

events.why: Rules are never deleted, and links from ADRs must keep working.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Every decision and amendment in an ADR numbered 0026 or higher has a `Rules:` line from the start. Older ADRs are checked once they have `Rules:` lines.

events.why: New ADRs shouldn't add to the backfill.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Whoever changes an ADR updates its rules in the same PR. The steward treats rules that don't match the ADR as a must-fix.

events.why: CI catches a registry left untouched; only a review catches one that says the wrong thing.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `pnpm rules:ship <version>` runs in the version PR. Each rule whose `target` is that version becomes `active`, with `since` set, a `shipped` event and no `target`.

events.why: Shipped events are generated, so a card's version can't be wrong.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `pnpm rules:build` writes `docs/rules/README.md`, which is committed: per concept, a table of rules, then each rule's history.

events.why: Agents and GitHub readers get every fact and every why in one file, with no tooling.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `pnpm rules:board` writes one self-contained page with the registry inlined to `.rules-board/index.html`, which is gitignored, and opens it. It has the Board, a rule drawer and the Agenda by day or by version.

events.why: The board is the view for reading across concepts and over time.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Rules for the existing ADRs are added one concept per PR, each reviewed by the maintainer. Supervision, Durability and Versioning & releases go first.

events.why: Each PR stays small enough to check against its ADRs.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `AGENTS.md` sends agents to `docs/rules/README.md` for what holds today.

events.why: Agents can't find the registry from the file tree alone.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: The registry covers this repo's ADRs only.

events.why: CI can only hold this repo's ADR PRs to their rules.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: The rules registry is internal tooling outside the milestones, and its PRs take the `no-changeset` label.

events.why: It ships nothing to npm and waits for no release.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: `rules:check` fails when a `decided` or `proposed` rule's `target` is at or below the packages' version. Previews such as `0.2.0-next.3` never trigger it.

events.why: The version PR that sets a version is where its rules ship.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A patch from a `release/0.x` branch gets its `shipped` events in that branch's version PR, and they come to `main` with the backport.

events.why: The branch is where the patch's version is set.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: A rule with `repo: true` is about how this repo works, not the published packages. It's `active` from its `built` event, has no `since`, `target` or `shipped` event, and `rules:ship` skips it.

events.why: Repo tooling and process never ship in an npm version, but they are in force once merged.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: Under an ADR's `## Decision`, a decision is a numbered `###` heading when there are any, otherwise a top-level numbered item, otherwise each `###` section. A heading that says "amended" is an amendment, and a `Rules:` line inside a code fence doesn't count.

events.why: The `Rules:` line check has to know which parts of an ADR need a line.
In force from the PR that built the rules registry.

statement: On a docs-only pull request, `check` runs in full and `cli-node24`, `browser`, `e2e` and `bench` report success without running their steps.

events.why: A docs change can't break runtime code, and the e2e and bench runs cost runner time for files they never read.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: A pull request is docs-only when every changed file is under `docs/`, `.changeset/` or `.claude/`, or ends in `.md`. Any other file makes it a full run.

events.why: An allowlist defaults to the full run, so a kind of file nobody listed never skips the tests.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: On a docs-only pull request the `e2e` jobs run and skip their steps, so `e2e (chromium)`, `e2e (firefox)` and `e2e (webkit)` still report as required checks.

events.why: A matrix job skipped as a whole reports one unexpanded `e2e` check, and the required names would stay pending.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: Only `pull_request` runs can be docs-only. Release dry runs and stage runs, the nightly, pushes and runs by hand always run every job they include.

events.why: A release run is the last full check before npm, so it must never skip.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: Every CI job, `bench` included, runs on `main` each night at 03:00 UTC, through `nightly.yml` calling `ci.yml`.

events.why: With docs-only PRs skipping e2e, a daily full run catches flaky tests, browser drift and interactions between PRs merged the same day; it replaces the weekly run.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: A scheduled nightly is skipped when `main` has no commits since the last green nightly. A nightly run by hand always runs.

events.why: A night with nothing new can only repeat the last result.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: A failed nightly opens an issue labelled `nightly-failure`, or comments on the open one, with the failed jobs and the commits since the last green nightly. The next green nightly closes it.

events.why: GitHub emails a failed scheduled run only to whoever last edited the workflow; an issue is seen by everyone, and the commit range points at the cause.
In force from the PR that built the docs-only skip and the nightly.

statement: We don't use `paths-ignore` or a path-filter action to skip CI for docs.

events.why: Why not just `paths-ignore`? The workflow wouldn't start, so the required checks would stay pending and the PR couldn't merge; a path-filter action is a dependency for a dozen lines of shell.
